3. How was the diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia confirmed in this patient?
Laboratory evaluation along with physical signs and symptoms can confirm a diagnosis of iron 
deficiency. Serum ferritin, iron, and total iron binding capacity (TIBC) were outside the normal 
reference range. A complete blood count revealed a microcytic anemia with a low mean corpus­
cular volume (MCV) of 82 fL. In this patient, serum ferritin was low at 7 ng/mL. Serum iron was 
low at 40 µg/dL, and TIBC was high at 425 µg/dL (the TIBC, or transferrin, concentration increases 
to compensate for low iron availability), confirming the diagnosis of iron deficiency. The patient’s 
hemoglobin, hematocrit, and MCV were low, indicating a microcytic anemia, and reticulocyte 
count was low, indicating decreased red blood cell production.
Serum ferritin is the single best non-invasive, sensitive marker of iron status. Serum ferritin 
concentrations reflect body iron stores (1 µg/L of serum ferritin concentration is equivalent to 
approximately 10 mg of stored iron). Compared to the gold standard of a bone marrow biopsy, 
serum ferritin is a sensitive and specific indicator of iron depletion. Levels below 15 mg/mL are
